related_questions.question: What's the quickest way to get rid of COVID symptoms?

text_blocks.snippet: The fastest way to recover from COVID-19 symptoms depends on the severity of the illness. For mild cases, rest, hydration, and over-the-counter medications like acetaminophen or ibuprofen can help manage symptoms. For those at higher risk, early treatment with medications like Paxlovid is crucial and must be started within 5-7 days of symptom onset to be effective, according to the CDC.
snippet_highlighted_words: rest, hydration, and over-the-counter medications like acetaminophen or ibuprofen

list.title: Rest:
list.snippet: Getting ample sleep (more than 7-9 hours) is essential for the body to recover, according to UnityPoint Health.

list.title: Over-the-counter medications:
list.snippet: Pain relievers and fever reducers like acetaminophen or ibuprofen can help manage symptoms like fever, aches, and pains.

list.title: Hydration:
list.snippet: Staying hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids is important.

list.title: Monitor symptoms:
list.snippet: Keep an eye on your symptoms and contact a doctor if they worsen or if you experience any emergency warning signs, says UnityPoint Health.

text_blocks.snippet: For those at higher risk (older adults, those with underlying conditions):

list.title: Early treatment:
list.snippet: If you are at higher risk, it's crucial to seek medical advice as soon as possible.

list.title: Antiviral medications:
list.snippet: Medications like Paxlovid can significantly reduce the risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death if started within the first 5-7 days of symptom onset.

related_questions.question: How long are you contagious with COVID?
related_questions.snippet: People with COVID-19 can be infectious from 1–2 days before and up to 8–10 days after symptoms begin. The majority of transmission appears to occur during the early periods of infection, particularly in the 1–2 days before symptoms start and within the first few days of symptom onset.

related_questions.question: What is the COVID anxiety syndrome?

text_blocks.snippet: COVID Anxiety Syndrome (CAS) is characterized by maladaptive coping strategies, such as avoidance and perseveration, in response to the perceived threat of COVID-19. It's a specific form of anxiety related to the pandemic, distinct from general anxiety about COVID-19. CAS can involve behaviors like excessive handwashing, social isolation, and constant checking for symptoms, even when not necessary.
snippet_highlighted_words: characterized by maladaptive coping strategies, such as avoidance and perseveration, in response to the perceived threat of COVID-19

list.title: Maladaptive Coping:
list.snippet: CAS involves unhelpful or excessive ways of dealing with the perceived threat of COVID-19.

list.title: Perseveration:
list.snippet: This refers to repetitive, often intrusive thoughts or actions related to the virus, like repeatedly checking for symptoms.

list.title: Avoidance:
list.snippet: Individuals with CAS may avoid situations or places they perceive as risky, even if those places are not actually dangerous.

list.title: Distinction from General Anxiety:
list.snippet: CAS is a specific type of anxiety related to the pandemic, rather than just general anxiety that may be present.

list.title: Potential for Persistence:
list.snippet: Even as the pandemic wanes, CAS can linger and affect individuals' lives.

text_blocks.snippet: While long COVID can also include anxiety and depression, CAS is distinct from the mental health impacts of the virus itself.
